# *CONFIDENTIAL — This document contains proprietary information intended solely for authorized Mercor contractors. By accessing this document, you agree to maintain strict confidentiality in accordance with your contractor agreement. Unauthorized disclosure, reproduction, or distribution is strictly prohibited.*

#  **Welcome\!**

You are joining a team of clinicians who guard the clinical simulations that frontier AI models are tested against.

You build the Worlds and design the Tasks within them — realistic patient cases with messy charts, conflicting specialist notes, and buried details, paired with clinical assignments an AI agent has to complete. You decide whether both are ready to teach an AI. Every scenario, every chart, every task, and every gold-standard response passes through your hands — and the ones that aren't strong enough don't move forward. Your decisions become the quality bar AI is held to.

Your success in this role is dependent on your clinical judgment and your eye for what makes a strong simulation. This document will teach you everything else. Read it carefully.

## **How to use this document**

This is your single source of truth for Project Sanctum. It follows the same sequence as your workflow — read it front to back the first time, then use it as a reference.

***Estimated reading time:** \~1 hour and 30 min*

| Section | What It Covers | Reading Time Estimate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **[Project Overview](#project-overview)** | What you're building and why | \~10 min |
| **[Getting Started](#getting-started)** | Setup, tools, policies | \~10 min |
| **[Phase 1 Part 1: Plan Your World](#heading=h.54d3l090prc4)** | Worlds, Tasks, Scenarios, Traps | \~20 min |
| **[Phase 2: Build Your Tasks](#phase-2:-build-your-tasks)** | Writing the task prompt, confirming the agent fails on it, and running initial QA reports |  \~20 min |
| **[Phase 3: QA Your Tasks](#heading=h.hus0sy5f11zm)** | Individual checks, snapshot health, environment linter, client review | \~15 min |
| **[Phase 4: Evaluate the Agent](#heading=h.hus0sy5f11zm)** | Failure analysis, preference ranking, submit for review | \~15 min |
| **[Appendix](#appendix)** | Concept deepdives, Examples, Claude Best Practices, FAQs | Reference only |

***Note**: Tabs specifically marked with 👣  highlight important step-by-step instructions\!*

- **Pgy-3 and above**

## **📚 Reading scope for new writers**

| 💡  Stop at the 🛑 ONBOARDING ENDS gate Read through the end of Phase 1 (Plan Your World). Phases 2–4 cover what veteran writers do after their first World Spec is approved. Focus on: Project Workflow → Phase 1: Plan Your World → Brainstorm → Section 1–4 of the World Spec. You must complete the Brainstorm and World Spec deliverables with sign-off from your assigned lead/reviewer before moving past onboarding. ## **Final Onboarding Deliverable: Your Paid Assessment**

Your contract will be capped at 1 hour. Additional payment for onboarding time will be subject to the completion and approval of a World Spec document.

* $2,000 \+ 1 hour of time from the contract — if your World Spec is approved (within up to 3 attempts)

* $500 \+ 1 hour of time from the contract — if you made an honest attempt but did not reach approval after all 3 attempts

An honest attempt means you showed initiative and followed instructions but could not reach an approved World Spec within 3 attempts.

| 💡  A note on good faith We trust everyone here to bring their best effort. Submissions that appear to game the system rather than engage in good faith will result in immediate offboarding with no additional payment. We don't anticipate this being an issue — just want to be upfront. 🤝 |
| :---- |

## **Timeline**

| ⚠  New writers have 1 week from signing their contract to get their World Spec approved. Writers who haven't submitted by then will be offboarded for inactivity. Need more time? Request an extension before the week ends and we'll work with you.  |

## **Project Communication — Slack**

Slack is the primary communication channel — small group channels, direct messages, and project-wide channels.

* Please respond within 24–36 hours. If you can't respond on time (vacation, clinical rotation), tell the team in advance

* Always opt to use a thread when posting — keeps channels clean and information consolidated

# 🤖 AI Usage Policy

# **AI Usage Policy**

| ⚠  AI \= LLM \= Claude. We are only using Claude for Project Sanctum. This policy governs how you use AI tools throughout Project Sanctum. Please use your PERSONAL EMAIL to sign up for Claude and upgrade to the $20 Pro version.  •  Post in the Slack Channel \#incentives-bonuses-tracker once paid to be reimbursed. You may use your personal email to bypass a known SSO blocker with mercor.expert emails. |
| :---- |

## **Three Non-Negotiables — 100% human-generated**

| 🚫 100% human-written | ✅ LLM-assisted is OK |
| :---- | :---- |
| Task Prompts | Brainstorming |
| Golden Responses | Boilerplate / drafting templates |
| Grader Guidelines | Consistency checking |

LLMs can support world-building, but the evaluation core itself must come from the physician expert. This is the foundation of the entire project.

## **Signs You're Approving Without Truly Reviewing**

Patterns that suggest critical review is being skipped:

| Sign | What it looks like |
| :---- | :---- |
| LLM-generated wo rding | Generic phrasing, AI tells, voice that doesn't match a real clinician |
| Timeline inconsistencies | Dates / chronology that conflict within or across documents |
| Typos and small errors | Errors a careful read-through would have caught |

| ⚠  Your professional judgment overrides AI — always. Some writers fall into the trap of treating AI's suggestions as instructions: accepting AI's framing because it sounds confident, redirecting their thinking because AI pushed back, or rewriting their work to match AI's preferred version. Don't. You are the senior clinician; AI is the assistant working for you. When AI suggests a direction that contradicts your professional judgment, follow your judgment — and push back on the AI. The training data we're producing is only as valuable as the expertise leading every decision. |
| :---- |

**There are no exceptions to these three.** LLMs can support world-building (brainstorming, boilerplate, consistency checking), but the evaluation core itself must come from the physician expert. This is the foundation of the entire project's integrity.See Claude **[Best Practices tab]()** in Appendix for guidance on using Claude effectively within these limits.

**Submitting Your Claude Transcripts**

You are required to submit your Claude conversation transcripts at **two** points during the workflow:

1. After completing **Phase 1** — submit the transcript from your world spec work.  
2. After completing **Phase 2** — submit the transcript from your task creation work.

When submitting, include which Claude product you used (e.g., Claude desktop app, Claude web version).

| ⚠  How to export your transcript: If you are using Claude desktop app: type / export in your conversation. This will generate a zip file of your transcript. If you are using Claude web version: go to Settings → Privacy, and click the "Export data" button. Once the export is processed, you will receive a download link via email. A few things to note: The download link expires 24 hours after delivery, and you must be signed in to your account to use it. This must be done from the desktop website — you cannot request exports from the iOS or Android apps. The export is all-or-nothing — you cannot select specific conversations. It includes your complete conversation history and account data. The data arrives as a ZIP file containing JSON. This is available to individual users on Free, Pro, and Max plans. Upload your exported zip file to the designated Google Drive folder. # 📚 Project Overview

# **Project Overview** {#project-overview}

## **🎯Our Goal on Project Sanctum**

Your role on Project Sanctum is of a **senior clinician**. You bring three things that AI cannot: the **clinical instinct** to imagine a realistic patient case, the **skill** to produce work that meets senior clinician standards, and the **judgment** to evaluate output against those standards. Across the workflow, you will design patient scenarios, produce senior-quality clinical work, and evaluate AI output against those standards.

Here's what we're working toward: today's best AI models still cannot reliably perform senior-quality clinical work. Project Sanctum helps train these models by placing them inside **realistic simulations** of clinical work environments, where they must complete the kind of assignments a practicing clinician would handle in real life.

Each **World** is one of these simulations: a realistic patient case containing multiple clinical tasks and the patient chart a clinician like you would navigate to complete them. An **AI agent** will attempt each task using only the documents in that chart. You then produce the **Golden Response** — the industry-standard deliverable a senior clinician would arrive at — and the gap between the agent's output and your answer becomes the training signal used to improve future models. The more realistic the World, the more valuable that signal becomes.

A fully realistic patient chart with many files and materials would take you many hours to build by hand — and most of those hours would go into producing documents that follow familiar structural patterns. Sanctum is designed so that this large-scale production can be handled efficiently by AI, while you focus your time on shaping the case itself: defining the clinical context, structuring the tasks, and ensuring the resulting environment reflects the complexity and messiness of real clinical practice.

| 💡  Our shared standards on Project Sanctum RealismThe scenarios, patient records, and clinical tasks you create should reflect what clinicians actually produce, work with, and complete in their day-to-day clinical practice. AI can only learn to do medical work if we train it on real medical work.  QualityAI models are only as strong as the data we give them. Your responsibility is making sure each deliverable is realistic and consistent with your World, using AutoQC \+ targeted spot-checks rather than full read-throughs. Attention to detailThe work is long, complex, and interconnected. AutoQC is embedded throughout this project to check and surface inconsistencies for you. Your job is to engage seriously with each finding: fix real issues, push back on false positives. The best experts treat AutoQC feedback as the trigger for their attention, not as something to skim past. Your judgment leadsWhen Claude suggests a direction that contradicts your professional judgment, follow your judgment. Claude doesn't know your clinical specialty; you do. ProfessionalismYou'll be reviewing each other's work, and disagreements will come up. Give each other the benefit of the doubt. When you flag a concern, be specific and constructive. When you receive feedback, engage with it seriously. When you and a reviewer disagree, escalate to a Team Lead with your reasoning — don't silently work around it. Direct, thoughtful dialogue is the norm here. |
| :---- |

## 

## **💡  The Driving Question**

| *How do I design a clinical environment that holds the workflows I’m required to complete, in a way that reflects the challenges of my day-to-day work and requires my expertise?* |
| :---: |

You know what professional-grade clinical work looks like — the format a senior clinician expects, the diagnostic depth patient safety requires, the judgment that comes from years of clinical practice. Think of the AI as **someone just starting in your domain** — freshly board-certified, or in their first year as a medical director — capable and knowledgeable, but without the seasoning that years in your specialty build. You're the seasoned one. The gap between someone just starting and someone seasoned is exactly the gap your tasks should expose.

## **The Three-Column Mental Model**

Three roles operate in parallel: the work you produce, what the AI does with it, and what we mean by "good." Hold all three columns in mind whenever you're designing.

| 1\. What you \+ AI produce | 2\. What the AI model does | 3\. What "good" means |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **A complete clinical environment package.** A realistic patient case (or multiple cases) and the surrounding clinical environment — including the scenario, multiple sources of information (EHR documents, patient-provided records, photos, external faxes, portal messages), patient records, and the clinical workflows that emerge from them. | An **AI Agent** attempts each clinical workflow by navigating the World files and working from the materials and instructions provided. | Everything you produce should be **realistic clinical work**, solvable by a strong clinician from the World files alone but too challenging for today's best AI to do well. |

## 

## **The Three Core Concepts**

Three concepts form the spine of the project: Scenario, Task, and World. They build on each other in an order, and understanding how they relate is the foundation everything else rests on.

| Concept | What it is | How you establish it  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **World** | The clinical environment you operate in — anchored in your role, your specialty, and the setting where you work. The World is the umbrella that holds your patient case, your clinical assignments, and the chart files the AI agent will navigate. | You start by naming your role ("I'm a hospitalist," "I'm a medical director in dermatology," "I'm an urgent care physician"). After your scenario and tasks are designed, the World *files* — the actual patient chart \+ any supporting documents — are generated and you review them before approving the build. |
| **Scenario** | A realistic patient case. It describes who the patient is, what their clinical situation is, and why care is happening now. | You brainstorm your patient case from your practice that fits your World — drawing from a case you'd realistically encounter in your role. |
| **Task** | A realistic clinical workflow an AI agent attempts to complete — the end-to-end work required to produce a specific deliverable (a discharge summary, a med reconciliation, a consult note, an RCA report). You'll design 8+ tasks per World, each mapped to one workflow on the approved list. | You sketch the 8+ workflows you'd realistically perform for that patient. |

## 

## **How to read AutoQC**

## AutoQC (Automated Quality Check) runs throughout your work on Sanctum from your Brainstorm to your final writeups. Three principles to keep in mind:

## **1\. AutoQC isn't perfect.** It can produce false positives: flagging things that aren't actually wrong, or missing things that are. When a finding feels off, trust your **clinical judgment** and push back with a clear justification.

## **2\. AutoQC isn't optional.** Every flag needs a response. Either agree (you'll fix the issue) or disagree and explain why AutoQC is wrong. Ignoring findings **blocks** your submission at later gates.

## **3\. AutoQC output isn't always intuitive.** Some findings are dense or technical. Spend a few minutes trying to understand each one. If you're still stuck, always feel free to ask your reviewer or pod lead. They are ready to help\!

## **Start with your role**

Before you brainstorm a scenario, sketch task ideas, or think about what materials or files belong in your World, anchor yourself in your role. Every clinician on this project comes in with a specialty and a setting — that's your starting point.

You might be a hospitalist managing inpatient admissions, a medical director reviewing peer cases, an urgent care physician handling walk-in evaluations, a dermatologist running an outpatient clinic, or a coding specialist auditing inpatient claims. Whatever your role is, that is the lens through which every design decision flows.

**Your role determines:**

* Which patient cases come to mind when you brainstorm your scenario

* Which workflows you'd realistically perform for that patient

* Which documents naturally exist in that working environment

* What "expert-quality" output looks like at the end

| 💡 A Simple Way to Think About this: 1\. Your role — "I am a \[specialty\] in \[setting\]." 2\. Your scenario — A patient case from my practice. 3\. Your tasks — The workflows I'd complete for that patient. 4\. Your World — The clinical environment that holds the case and supports the tasks. |
| :---- |

## 

## **How a World Comes Together**

Here is the full sequence from start to finish. AI does the heavy drafting throughout; your role is to design, decide, and review.

| Make a plan                       ← design your scenario \+ task ideas        ↓ Build your World                  ← the patient chart \+ any additional materials                                       generated from your plan        ↓ Review the built World            ← confirm realism and complexity |
| :---- |

Pipeline Fixes \= 5 hours 1 Task (end-to-end) \= 8-10 hours (Note: This includes revisions and communication with reviewer/pod lead/EPM). Task Prompt / Golden Response \= 1 hour  Grader Guidelines \= 30 mins Failure Analysis (FA) \= 1 hour Grader feedback/analysis (GA) \= 30-45 mins Preference label x 3 \= 1-1.5 hours |

## **Production Pipeline \- 4 Phases, 17 Steps**

### **Phase 1 — Plan your world  (Steps 1–6)**

| \# | Step | What happens | Tools |
| ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | **Brainstorm** | High-level plan for world design and task ideas. Posted for pod lead or peer review per current channel norms. | RL Studio, Slack |
| 2 | **Brainstorm AutoQC** | Automated quality check to confirm the brainstorm is robust and complete prior to human review. | RL Studio |
| 3 | **Human Review (Brainstorm)** | Pod lead or peer reviewer signs off. Two types of results: **Pass** or **Send for edits**. You address any audit items before moving forward. | RL Studio, Slack |
| 4 | **World Spec Document \+ Reference Templates** | Develop the full world specification AND curate the Reference Templates folder using Claude. The Claude Project workflow will be explained in the [template & reference guide](). Both are uploaded together to RL Studio as a single package. | RL Studio |
| 5 | **World Spec AutoQC** | Automated check that the world spec and Reference Templates folder follow requirements for successful synthetic generation. | RL Studio |
| 6 | **Human Review (World Spec \+ Templates)** | Reviewer / lead approves both the spec and the Reference Templates folder before engineering handoff. Approval at this gate is the trigger for synthetic generation. | RL Studio |
| **ONBOARDING ENDS HERE** |  |  |  |

### **Phase 2 — Build your files & Tasks  (Steps 7–9)**

| \# | Step | What happens | Tools |
| ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 7 | **Synthetic Generation Pipeline** | Engineering's iterative pipeline auto-extracts the approved spec and Reference Templates folder and generates the world synthetic files. | RL Studio (engineering) |
| 8 | **World AutoQC** | Automated check on file integrity, schema, and world consistency. Loops back to Step 7 on failure. | RL Studio |
| 9 | **Writer Reviews Files** | Writer reviews the generated files. Minor issues edited in place. Files too far from fixable are resubmitted to the AI Build Pipeline to regenerate (back to Step 7). Writer approved world files in the end, and final review are done by pod lead / Team Lead / reviewer | RL Studio |
| **Writers with Approved Spec moved from New Writer to a MAIN POD** |  |  |  |

### **Phase 3 — Write Your Tasks and Run QC (Steps 10–13)**

| \# | Step | What happens | Tools |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 10 | **Set Up Tasks in RL Studio (incl. task writing)** | Upload task files, draft the task prompt, golden response, and grader guidelines directly in RL Studio. Save after every step. | RL Studio |
| 11 | **Task AutoQC (post-setup)** | Automated check on overall task quality. Runs immediately after task setup at Step 10\. Writer addresses findings before running the agent. | RL Studio |
| 12 | **Run the Agent** | Run all tasks and wait for output. A full run typically takes \~1 hour. | RL Studio |
| 13 | **Taiga QC** | Trajectory \+ grading audit. Writer addresses findings. | Taiga / RL Studio |

### **Phase 4 — Evaluate the AI Agent  (Steps 14–17)**

| \# | Step | What happens | Tools |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 14 | **Failure Analysis (FA) \+ Grader Analysis (GA)** | Compare the lowest-scoring trajectory to the golden response. Document clinical, administrative, and style errors. Write the FA paragraph and the Grader Analysis paragraph. | RL Studio / Taiga |
| 15 | **Preference Labeling (PL)** | Compare two attempts (A vs B). Select the preferred attempt. Write the justification across the seven-section format. | RL Studio / Taiga |
| 16 | **AutoQC on FA \+ PL** | Automated quality check on the FA writeup and the PL justifications. Confirms adherence to the major components required for FA, Grader Analysis, and PL. | RL Studio |
| 17 | **Final Reviewer Review** | Final human review to confirm every prior audit item has been addressed and the task is ready for delivery. Reviewer may be a Team Lead, pod lead, or EPM. | RL Studio |

## **Sanctum Coach core features** {#sanctum-coach-core-features}

* **Teaches at your pace.** It explains one concept at a time and calibrates to what you already know, moving faster when you have it and slowing down when you do not.  
* **Answers any question, any time.** Ask it to clarify any concept (friction vs trap, world snapshot, self-containment, task independence) whenever you are unsure. It teaches through your questions.  
* **Explains workflows you do not recognize.** Not sure what an approved workflow involves? Just ask. It gives a plain-language explanation so you can pick the right one with confidence.  
* **Suggests fitting workflows from the current approved list.** It pulls the live, always-up-to-date workflow list and proposes options tailored to your scenario, grouped by category and priority (P0/P1/P2). Aim for variety: at least 3 distinct workflows, and more is better when each genuinely fits.  
* **Helps you design the hard parts.** Frictions vs traps, the world timeline and snapshot, keeping tasks independent (no task builds on another), self-containment, and making each task genuinely difficult.  
* **Flags the rules upfront.** It tells you at the start that the entire case must take place before July 2025 (the model's knowledge cutoff), and catches common mistakes early (mid-timeline tasks, look-alike tasks, non-physician framing) before they cost you time.  
* **Assembles your deliverable and self-checks it.** It builds your brainstorm or spec from your own ideas in the required format, walks the draft against the pre-submission QC checklist so you know it would pass, and gives you the handoff steps.  
* **Helps curate templates.** In Template Curation it matches each world file to a databank template, a public-domain form, or a custom template, keeps filenames consistent, and flags any media you must create yourself.

| For any questions in the brainstorm, world spec, and template curation phases, ask Sanctum Coach first\! It will give you an instant response and provide additional guidance personalized to you. |

## 

## **Template curation detailed steps** {#template-curation-detailed-steps}

This phase works differently from Brainstorm and World Spec. Instead of teaching concepts, the Coach builds your **Reference Templates** folder with you and **produces files for you to download**. **Do it right after you draft your World Spec.**

1. Open a new chat and say you are on Template Curation. Paste your World Spec so the Coach knows which files your world needs.  
2. **Upload your DataBank file (Template\_DataBank.docx) into the chat**. The Coach reads it directly to pull each template with its original formatting. This one upload is what makes template creation work.  
3. The Coach goes through your world-level files one at a time and handles each by type:  
   1. **DataBank match:** it extracts that template from your DataBank and gives you a downloadable, fully-formatted .docx. Just download it.  
   2. **Custom (no match):** it drafts one with you in the standard clinical format and gives you a downloadable .docx.  
   3. **Public-domain form:** it names the official source; you download the blank form from there.  
   4. **Writer-produced (EKG, photo, audio, lab or imaging output):** the Coach cannot make these. It lists which ones you must create yourself with the specialty tools, and can write you a generation prompt if you ask.  
4. **Download every file the Coach produces**, add any forms or media you sourced, and keep them together as your **Reference Templates** folder.  
5. **Upload** that Reference Templates folder together with your World Spec to RL Studio, then run World Spec AutoQC.

| Tip: keep each file named the way the Coach names it, so it matches your World Spec file plan. |

# **🧠 Brainstorm Your World**

**→ Pipeline Steps 1–3**

Now that you've internalized Scenario, Task, and World, you're ready for your first deliverable: the Brainstorm — a short concept pitch capturing your scenario, your 8+ task sketches, and how they fit together. This is where you lock in conceptual viability before you spend hours on the World Spec.

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your brainstorm work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create a brainstorm. |
| :---- |

## **Overview of Goals**

| Goal | Action |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Open Claude Project |
| 2 | Walk through 4-element pitch with Claude: World setup, Major frictions, Major traps, Rough task ideas |
| 3 | Run informal Self-QC with Claude before submitting (optional but encouraged) |
| 4 | Submit Brainstorm to RL Studio for AutoQC |
| 5 | Post in pod channel \+ tag pod lead for Human Review |
| 6 | Address any review feedback; resubmit if needed |

**Working with Claude**

Use Claude as a thinking partner — sketch scenario, stress-test task ideas, identify gaps. Claude helps you iterate quickly. 

| Element | What to bring | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. World setup** | Who the patient is and what clinical situation the world represents: •  Demographics and comorbidities •  Clinical environment (specialty, inpatient vs. outpatient vs. administrative oversight) •  Encounter type (admission, clinic visit, RCA review, peer review, coding audit, and so on) •  Shape of the timeline; what changes over the course of the world Enough to know the world is medically and contextually coherent. | *"This is an inpatient hospital medicine world: a \[N\]-day admission for \[presenting problem\] in a \[age\] \[sex\] with \[comorbidities\]."* *"This is an outpatient primary care world: a single clinic visit for \[chief complaint\] in a \[age\] \[sex\] with \[relevant chronic conditions\]."* *"This is a medical director world: an RCA review of \[event type\] involving a \[age\] \[sex\] who \[outcome\]; reviewer has access to chart and incident materials."* |
| **2\. Major friction points** | Opposing forces, viewpoints, or stakeholder positions that complicate the scenario: •  Two specialists with conflicting recommendations •  Family wishes vs. medical recommendation •  Primary team vs. consultant disagreement  ⚠️**Frictions are about people and perspectives. Traps (next row) are about information.** | *"Cardiology and nephrology disagree on whether to hold the ACE inhibitor."* *"Family wants comfort care; the primary team is still pursuing aggressive workup."* *"PCP recommends one regimen at clinic; the inpatient team has a different plan at admission."*  |
| **3\. Major traps** | Nuggets of information or specific incidents that complicate the clinician's job and can lead to incorrect decisions if not contextualized properly.  **Common trap types:** •  Contradictory EMR information •  Buried clinically significant information •  Insufficient or missing patient information •  Source-of-truth ambiguity •  Social determinants of health •  Temporal or sequencing complexity | *"Stale EMR med list contradicts a recently filled pill bottle photo. Source-of-truth ambiguity. Lives in the med rec task only."* *"Aspiration event documented mid-paragraph in a routine nursing note, never escalated. Buried significant information. World-level trap."* *"Caregiver burnout limits adherence and follow-up capacity. SDOH trap. World-level, affects every task that touches the discharge plan."* |
| **4\. Rough task ideas** | The clinical workflows the writer is thinking about as task encounters. Each task is independent and lives temporally after the world. For each task: the deliverable type and which world elements, traps, or frictions it would test. **Reference the team's approved workflows tracker**:[Project\_Sanctum\_Approved\_Task\_Selection\_Categories\_06.13.2026 (1).pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1U7SnCcFPfl0sErYGkD0ZoU7otncLY__7/view?usp=drive_link)  for the full list of validated deliverable types. The categories below are a representative sample to encourage thinking beyond progress notes and discharge medication lists. •  Direct clinical documentation (H\&P, progress note, discharge summary, consult, SOAP, op note) •  Medication, coding, & billing (med rec, ICD-10/CPT crosswalk, prior auth, denial appeal) •  Care transitions & coordination (transfer note, post-discharge follow-up, home health plan, hospice/palliative) •  Quality, safety, & oversight (RCA, sentinel event, M\&M, peer review, OPPE/FPPE, utilization review) •  Administrative-clinical hybrid (FMLA, disability, ADA accommodation, return-to-work, workers' comp, SAP) •  Specialty evaluation & legal-medical (VA disability, SSDI, IME, pre-op clearance, school medical form) | *"Task 1 is a discharge medication reconciliation. Draws on the three-way med discrepancy and the buried dose change. Set at hospital day 7, which is the final day of the world."* *"Task 2 is a pre-operative clearance note. Draws on the cardiology/nephrology friction and the chronic disease profile. Set 2 weeks after the last day of the clinical timeline (discharge date)."* *"Task 3 is the RCA write-up itself (medical director world). Draws on every friction and trap. Set 4 weeks after the index event."* |

| 💡  Friction vs Trap — they're not interchangeable Friction \= stated dilemma; the disagreement is on the chart and the agent has to weigh competing perspectives. Trap \= hidden issue; the agent has to notice the problem first. Both belong in a strong World, but they live in different design spaces. |
| :---- |

## 

## **What the lead evaluates**

Walk through the checklist below, organized to mirror the writer's four elements. Send back if any item is a clear no.

| World setup Patient and clinical situation are coherent. The patient/scenario could exist; specialty, environment, encounter type, and timeline are clear and internally consistent. Patient profile fits the encounter. Realistic in the sense that a domain expert has encountered this patient several times in their career. Major friction points Frictions realistically represent real-world clinical dilemmas. Writer can name the stakeholders involved and what each is advocating for. Major traps There are a variety of traps in the world that altogether create enough clinical complexity that can stump a physician under normal circumstances. Rough task ideas Each task maps to a deliverable type in the team's approved workflows tracker. Tasks also have their own “traps” that are distinct from the world-level traps.  Cross-cutting Writer has answers for potential issues of self-containment that can arise.  A seasoned clinician could solve every task from the intended files alone. Overall world design is representative of the daily activities of a physician in that domain.  |
| :---- |

| DO | DON'T |
| :---- | :---- |
| **✓**  Start with YOUR clinical pain points — "the cases that drive me up the wall." | **✗**  Start with a textbook diagnosis or a zebra. "This patient has 5 rare conditions" creates fake complexity. **✗**  Stack rare diseases. Real complexity is HFrEF \+ pAF \+ CKD \+ COPD \+ DM \+ obesity, not 5 zebras. |
| **✓**  Aim for multiple comorbidities, long medication lists. Complexity from common conditions intersecting. | **✗** Use a patient case who is a 25 year old male with an unremarkable past medical and surgical history and only takes Zyrtec for allergies.   |
| **✓**  Include 2+ real frictions — specialist vs specialist, family vs team, PCP vs admitting. | **✗**  Confuse frictions with traps. Specialist disagreement \= friction. Buried lab finding \= trap |
| **✓**  Make sure you have both world-level and task-level traps that are” reasonably ambiguous” but still fair game | **✗**  Have traps that are glaringly obvious that the model will immediately pick up on them  |
| **✓**  Map every task to a P0/P1/P2 workflow on the approved tracker. At least one P0. | **✗**  Invent a workflow. If your task doesn't fit, ask in Slack. |

# ⚠️ Workflow Selection

# **Selecting Workflows**

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your brainstorm work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create a brainstorm. |
| :---- |

Every World contains **5-8+ tasks** spanning different clinical workflows. This tab shows you how to pick.

### **The Workflow List👇**

[Project\_Sanctum\_Approved\_Task\_Selection\_Categories\_06.13.2026 (1).docx](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_-2_P0j2nP0eEaQMjt0jdrYnalMXyQr2/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=111631573631761265982&rtpof=true&sd=true) — the maintained list of approved workflows \+ priorities.

Workflows are prioritized:

* **P0** \= high priority (start here)  
* **P1** \= medium priority (acceptable if P0 is exhausted)  
* **P2** \= low priority (acceptable if P0 and P1 are exhausted)

| ⚠  At least one task per World must use a P0 workflow. |
| :---- |

### **Why workflows span multiple domains**

In practice, physicians wear multiple hats. Your day-to-day mix can include:

* **Clinical** documentation (progress notes, discharge summaries, consults)  
* **Healthcare admin** (prior auth, coding/billing, utilization review)  
* **Quality / safety / oversight** (RCA, peer review, M\&M)  
* **Educational** \+ **specialty-specific** workflows

Sanctum tasks should reflect this real-world breadth.

### **Rules of thumb**

| Rule | Value |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Total tasks per World** | 8+ |
| **Distinct workflows per World** | At least 3–5 |
| **Workflow repetition** | Allowed — same workflow can appear multiple times, as long as the 3–5 distinct minimum is met |
| **At least 1 P0 workflow** | Required |
| **Mix of clinical \+ admin** | Recommended |

### **Example: 8-task World**

| \# of Tasks | Workflow |
| ----- | ----- |
| 3 | Ambulatory Clinical Progress Note Documentation (SOAP Notes) |
| 2 | Discharge Medication Reconciliation |
| 2 | Prior Authorization Request and Management |
| 1 | Hospital Discharge Summary Generation |

**Total: 4 distinct workflows across 8 tasks.** SOAP notes repeat 3× — that's fine, because the overall workflow count clears the 3–5 minimum.

## **Who Reads Your World Spec**

Your world specification document serves two audiences, and understanding this will help you write it well.

1. **AI Build pipeline.** The pipeline auto-extracts your spec and your Reference Templates folder to generate the actual world files (lab reports, progress notes, imaging reports, medication lists, and every other clinical document in the patient chart). The spec needs enough clinical detail and internal consistency to produce realistic files. If your spec says the patient has CKD Stage 3b with a baseline Cr of 1.5, every downstream file must reflect that.

2. **Other clinicians.** Once your world is built, other writers may add tasks to it. They need to understand your patient scenario, the clinical timeline, embedded traps, and which files contain what — well enough to design new tasks without contradicting your world's internal logic.

Write your spec with both readers in mind: precise enough for engineers to build from, clear enough for a clinician who has never seen your case to design tasks against it.

## **World Spec Rule of Thumb**

Your narrative content: scenario, parties, transaction, task designs, and file plan. The template uses bold lead-in labels for each field. Replace the placeholder text with your own content.

| Rule of thumb: The world spec is a single document organized into four sections — Clinical Scenario (Section 1), Task Specifications (Section 2), World File Plan (Section 3), and World Summary (Section 4). Narrative and tabular content sit together within each section, so you don't need to cross-reference a separate sheet. This document is the single source of truth for your world. Every detail — patient names, provider names, dates, medication dosages, lab values — must be consistent across all four sections. A date in your Key Milestones table (Section 1.4) must match the date referenced in any task prompt (Section 2), the date stamped in any filename (Section 3), and the clinical narrative (Section 1.3). Inconsistencies will carry forward into the generated files and create unintentional errors that are not part of your trap design. |
| :---- |

### **Working with Claude**

Claude dramatically speeds up the mechanical work of drafting your spec. But it's a tool, not a collaborator.  
💡 **You are the pilot. Claude is the plane.** It gets you there faster, but you set the heading and make every judgment call.  
What Claude CAN'T do

| Claude can't... | What this means for you |
| :---- | :---- |
| Judge whether a task is realistic for your specialty | Claude will generate task descriptions that sound plausible but no physician in your area would actually perform that way. You apply that filter |
| Assess difficulty from a domain expert's perspective | A task that looks hard to Claude may be trivial to a clinician — and vice versa. Calibrate: would a non-specialist get this right on the first pass? If yes, it's too easy |
| Verify traps are genuinely misleading | Claude can structure a trap, but only you can judge whether a clinician in your area would actually be misled by it |
| Push back without being asked | Explicitly ask it to challenge your assumptions: "Is this task too easy?", "Does this file earn its place?", "What's the plausible wrong answer here and why would a careful reader reach it?" |

⚠️ You must carefully review all Claude outputs. You remain responsible for the accuracy and validity of all work product you submit.

# 1️⃣ Clinical Scenario

## **Section 1: Clinical Scenario** 

**→ World Spec Template, Section 1: Clinical Scenario**

This is where you spec your patient and their clinical course. **A reader with no context should understand your world in under 60 seconds after reading Section 1\.**

Most of the clinical thinking already happened in your **Brainstorm** — patient case, clinical context, key players, precipitating event. Section 1 turns those sketches into a formal spec with five sub-sections of detail.

**Claude** handles most of Section 1's mechanical drafting — structuring the patient profile table, drafting the clinical history narrative, populating the milestones table, writing the complexity analysis. 

Your job is to **direct \+ review**: confirm clinical accuracy, surface anything Claude missed, and make sure facts are internally consistent.

| ⚠   Source of truth for the whole World. Every fact referenced anywhere downstream — task prompts, file plan, Failure Design — must trace back to Section 1.3 (Clinical History) or Section 1.4 (Key Milestones). If a date doesn't appear in 1.4, it can't appear in a task prompt. If a comorbidity isn't in 1.2 or 1.3, it can't show up in a consult note. Inconsistency here cascades into every downstream file and task. |
| :---- |

## **Claude can draft most of Section 1\. Your job: clinical accuracy \+ internal consistency**

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your world spec work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create world spec \+ templates. |
| :---- |

| What | Claude does | You do |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Big Picture Summary (1.1)** | Drafts one paragraph from your Brainstorm | Confirm it captures the essence; reads in under 60 seconds |
| **Patient Profile (1.2)** | Structures the demographic \+ clinical identity table | Verify clinical accuracy — comorbidities, meds, doses match real practice |
| **Clinical History (1.3)** | Drafts continuous narrative from your Brainstorm | Verify every fact is clinically plausible; this becomes your source of truth |
| **Key Milestones (1.4)** | Structures the Date / Event / Anchor table | Decide which dates anchor traps and tasks; verify internal consistency |
| **Clinical Complexity (1.5)** | Drafts the analysis | Confirm complexity emerges from realistic combinations, not rare diagnoses or trick wording |
| **Optional 1.2 sub-tables** | Structures any sub-table you tell it to add | Decide which sub-tables to add (med list / hospital course / friction / hierarchy) |

## **Optional sub-tables under 1.2 — add when relevant**

* **Home Medication List** — if the world tests medication reconciliation or polypharmacy  
* **Hospital Course Timeline** — multi-day admissions or perioperative sequences  
* **Decision Friction Table** — competing pathways the model must choose between (Friction Point | Options | Correct Pathway)  
* **Data Hierarchy Note** — when source-of-truth ranking matters (e.g., attending \> specialist \> note \> family report \> EMR)

# 2️⃣ Task Specification

## **Section 2: Task Specifications**

**→ World Spec Template, Section 2: Task Specifications**

This is where you place your 8+ task ideas. Each task needs five spec fields that together define what the agent does, what success looks like, and where it can fail.

Most of the clinical thinking already happened in your **Brainstorm** — workflows, rough task ideas, major traps, frictions. Stage 2 turns those sketches into a formal spec. The biggest **new** work here is writing each **Task Prompt** — the naturalistic clinical request the agent will see. Everything else is making your Brainstorm sketches more precise and assignable. 

Claude handles the mechanical scaffolding around your work: structuring rows, pulling workflow names from your Brainstorm, cross-checking dates and file IDs, refining wording on prompts you've already drafted.

| ⚠   What the agent sees vs. what's metadata. Only the Draft Prompt is sent to the AI agent that will attempt your task later. Workflow names, Expected Output structure, and Failure Design are spec metadata — they help reviewers and graders, not the agent. Letting any of this leak into the prompt spoon-feeds the model and lowers our failure-rate signal. |
| :---- |

### 

### **Claude can help most of Stage 2's mechanical work. Three things must come from you.**

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your world spec work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create world spec \+ templates. |
| :---- |

| What | Claude does | You do |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Task Prompt** ⚠️ human-written | Refines / polishes wording **after you've drafted** | Write each prompt from scratch — your clinical voice |
| **Failure Design / Traps** ⚠️ human-written | (cannot generate from scratch) | Design each trap from your clinical judgment |
| **Expected Output** ⚠️ human-written | (cannot — defines the Golden Response) | Articulate the anchors a grader will check |
| **Workflow** | Pulls names from the approved list | Pick which workflows; enforce P0 \+ clinical/admin mix （at least 3-5 types) |
| **Spec rows / table format** | Structures the 5-field rows | Verify structure is correct |
| **Date consistency** | Cross-checks dates against Section 1.4 (Key Milestones) | Confirm dates align with your scenario |
| **File ID consistency** | Verifies E\#-T\# IDs match Section 3 | Ensure correct file naming |
| **Temporality** | Can flag if anchor date sits in the World window | Decide the anchor date (always Day 8+ after World ends) |
| **Gradability** | (cannot — Expected Output anchors are yours) | Confirm you can articulate the correct output as a concrete deliverable |

| 💡  Two file scopes you'll see in Field 5 World-level files are visible to every task in your World — the base clinical environment (chart, progress notes, labs, consult notes, medication lists, etc.) that any task may reference. Task-level files are scoped to one specific task — inputs that wouldn't realistically live in the longitudinal chart (a referring physician email, prior auth form, RCA meeting minutes, ambient scribe audio). If a task only needs the base chart, it uses world-level files only and Field 5 reads "None. World-level files only." Detailed file planning happens in Stage 3.1. |
| :---- |

## 

## **The Five Spec Fields**

| Field | What it contains | What to check in Claude's draft | Example (from World 004, Task 2\) |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Workflow** | A workflow name from the approved [Workflow List](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YRUwLm3oLjlL2v2g-_lw9rC_NeJ5gcpHBX6_M_HHh4c/edit) plus a one-line context — who's doing it, in what setting (e.g., "Night float resident preparing discharge medication reconciliation"). | Workflow is on the approved list. At least **one P0** workflow \+ mix (**3-5 types**) of clinical and healthcare-admin workflows across your 8+ tasks | "Diagnostic Coding Crosswalk — OEM physician building ICD-10/VASRD/ICD-11 codes for VA disability evaluation" |
| **Draft Prompt** | The prompt sent to the AI agent. Written in the voice of the clinician/user issuing the request — naturalistic, with clinical context, documents attached, and constraints mentioned. The **temporal anchor** (date / hospital day) embedded naturally through the timestamp, the user's framing, or the attached documents. | Reads like a **real request** from a real person, not a test question. Anchor date sits AFTER the World's reality window. No leakage of expected output or trap design | "In anticipation for his C\&P medical exams and overall application for service connection, you want to make sure that you have the correct ICD-10 codes and the corresponding VASRD codes for Mr. Caduceus. You also want to add ICD-11 codes in a separate column. Build an ICD-10 / VASRD / ICD-11 coding crosswalk table as an addendum to this veteran's VA disability evaluation. For each condition, provide the appropriate ICD-10-CM code, VASRD diagnostic code, and ICD-11 code, with clinical rationale citing specific findings from the source files." |
| **Expected Output** | The deliverable: format, length, register, and the specific clinical content that constitutes a correct response. Name the key anchors a grader will check. This is the basis for the **Golden Response** you'll write in Phase 2\. | Precise enough that you could write a Golden Response from this description alone. If you can't, the task isn't ready | "9-row, 6-column table (\#, Condition, Clinical Basis, ICD-10-CM, VASRD, ICD-11 MMS). 2 pre-existing rows \+ 7 newly recommended rows (bilateral knees split for separate VASRD coding). 27 gradable code cells \+ 9 clinical basis citations. Key assignments: PTSD F43.10/9411/6B40, OSA G47.33/6847/7A41.0, IHD I25.119/7005/BA40.Z..." |
| **Failure Design** | 5–6 highest-yield traps per task in a two-column table: **Key Trap** (what will mislead the AI agent) \+ **Remediation** (what the correct response does and why). Full trap inventories live in your working spec; only highest-yield ones go in the spec doc. | Each trap is clinically plausible, discoverable from World files, and produces a meaningful clinical error when missed. Cross-document reasoning required (see Brainstorm template trap guidance) | **Key Trap:** "Classification system conflation" **Remediation:** "VASRD is functional-impairment indexed; ICD-10 is etiology-and-anatomy indexed. Reason about each system independently" |
| **Task-level files** | Files scoped to this task using the **E\#-T\#** convention (e.g., E1-T3 \= first essential file for Task 3). If only world-level files apply, write "None. World-level files only." | File IDs match Section 3 (File Plan). Reuse across tasks is fine — note it; reuse doesn't violate task independence because tasks grade as separate evaluation runs | "None. World-level files only." *(For tasks with task-level files: "E1-T6 \= Pill\_Bottles\_Photo\_Caduceus.jpg")* |

# 3️⃣ World File Plan

## **Section 3: World File Plan \+ Reference Templates** 

**→ World Spec Template, Section 3: World File Plan**

This is where you fill in **Section 3 of the World Spec** — the full inventory of documents your World will contain. Each file gets a row in an 8-column table that engineering reads programmatically.

Your Brainstorm gave you a rough sense of what your World needs (progress notes, consults, labs, etc.). Stage 3.1 turns that sketch into a formal, assignable file list with IDs, filenames, dates, sources, descriptions, and trap assignments.

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your world spec work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create world spec \+ templates. |
| :---- |

### **Two distinctions of files you'll work with**

| 💡 Essential vs Supplementary Essential — files required for at least one task; may carry trap content. \~90% of your World. Supplementary — files that add realistic clinical noise but carry no trap content. \~10% of your World. Litmus test: if removing the file would not change any correct answer for any task, it's supplementary. |
| :---- |

| 💡 World-level vs Task-level World-level — designed to be visible to every task (the base chart: progress notes, labs, consult notes, medication lists). Task-level — scoped to a specific task, typically added to the prompt itself in order to ensure self-containment or reflect real-world cognitive-noise (e.g. a last minute photo given to the E.R. physician, recent patient portal message, publicly-released Leapfrog hospital patient safety data, etc.) |
| :---- |

# 

# **Claude can draft most of Stage 3.1. Two things must come from you**

| What | Claude does | You do |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **What's Essential vs Supplementary** ⚠️ your call | Drafts file rows | Decide which files carry traps / are required for tasks (essential) vs realistic noise (supplementary) |
| **Where traps live in files** ⚠️ your call | (cannot — traps are clinical judgment) | Specify which file carries which trap from Section 2 Failure Design; fill the Pearls/Traps/Friction Part 2 |
| **Row drafts (7-column)** | Drafts rows from your Brainstorm \+ Section 2 tasks | Verify clinical accuracy \+ cross-section consistency |
| **Naming conventions (EW\# / E\#-T\# / WS\# / TS\#)** | Applies systematically across rows | Spot-check final IDs |
| **Filenames with datestamps** | Generates from Section 1.4 (Key Milestones) | Confirm dates align with MM.DD.YYYY format |
| **Reference File Origin** | Suggests source from Public Domain / Custom Template / Databank Template /Writer-produced | Confirm source choice; detailed curation workflow lives in **3.2 Template/Reference File Guide** |

# 

# **The 7-column row structure**

| Column | What goes in it |
| ----- | ----- |
| **1\. \#** | Sequential row number. Restart at the top of each sub-section |
| **2\. ID** | Per the naming conventions above (EW\# / E\#-T\# / WS\# / TS\#) |
| **3\. Filename.type** | Final synthetic filename engineering will produce, **with datestamp** (MMDDYYYY) \+ extension. Example: `DischargeSummary_04262026.docx` |
| **4\. Date** | **MM.DD.YYYY** format. Must match a date in Section 1.4 (Key Milestones) |
| **5\. Reference File Origin** | One of four: **Public Domain** (existing form, e.g., FMLA / OSHA), **Custom Made** (you draft template from scratch, engineering converts), **Databank Template** (Mercor's internal template library), **Writer-produced file** (not a template, engineering does NOT touch).  Detailed curation workflow lives in **3.2 Template/Reference File Guide** |
| **6\. Description** | Detailed specification: clinical content to include, clinical content to **exclude**, format/layout requirements. **NOT** "Standard progress note" — specify key content, structure, specific findings or language to include |
| **7\. Pearls, Traps, and Friction** | **Two parts:** **Part 1** (pearls): What function does this file serve for the patient? What clinical pearls would a physician reading it learn? **Part 2** (traps/frictions): What traps live in this file, mapped to Section 2 Failure Design? What points of friction between stakeholders are surfaced? **For supplementary files, Part 2 \= N/A** (supplementary files carry no traps) |

## **What to check in Claude's draft**

- [ ] Every essential file has a clear connection to a task (cross-check Section 2 task-file mapping)  
- [ ] Every supplementary file carries no trap content (Pearls/Traps/Friction Part 2 \= N/A)  
- [ ] File descriptions are detailed enough that a builder with no clinical training could produce them ("Standard progress note" is not enough)  
- [ ] Every date in Filename.type / Date columns appears in Section 1.4 (Key Milestones)  
- [ ] IDs follow the naming convention systematically across all rows  
- [ ] The 90/10 ratio is approximately maintained  
- [ ] The full Section 3 inventory is realistic — would a clinician working on this patient have these files in the chart?  
- [ ] Pearls/Traps/Friction Part 2 traps map cleanly back to Section 2 Failure Design

## **Example row (from World 004 — essential world-level)**

| \# | ID | Filename.type | Date | Reference File Origin | Description | Pearls, Traps, and Friction |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| 5 | EW5 | Echo\_TTE\_11042023..docx | 11.04.2023 | Databank Template | Transthoracic echocardiogram report. Standard structure: demographics, indication ("evaluate LV function for SOB workup"), findings (LVEF 50–55% mildly reduced, mild LVH, mild MR, normal RV), conclusion. Reading cardiologist signature/date. Do NOT include any post-2023 findings | Part 1: Establishes LVEF anchor for IHD service connection determination (Task 1). Clinical pearl: borderline LVEF requires careful rating logic under VASRD DC 7005\. Part 2: LVEF 50–55% sits at the rating boundary between VASRD codes — agent must reason carefully about which side it falls on (Trap from Task 1 Failure Design). |

**For images, audio, and other custom artifacts, you generate these yourself or source reputable, publicly available materials.**

⚠️ NOTE: It is critical that your traps are integrated into your synthetic files in a 'reasonably ambiguous' fashion (not glaringly obvious) so that the clinical complexity remains while still considered fair game for any seasoned physician expert to solve. For example, if a trap implies the patient is prediabetic in a progress note, the HPI should state the patient had an A1c of 5.8%, not blatantly say 'Mr. Jones is prediabetic.  
'

File naming. Keep it simple and intuitive. Avoid overly detailed naming conventions. Simpler names help the model understand and look up information more effectively.

Every essential file in the spec should include either a reference document link with usage instructions, or a description detailed enough for a non-domain-expert builder to draft it. 'Standard progress note' is not enough. Specify key clinical content, structure, and any specific findings or language that must be included.

# 🗃️ Template & Reference Guide

**Template/Reference File Curation Guide**

**→ Goes into your Reference Templates folder → uploaded with World Spec at RL Studio Step**

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your world spec work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create world spec \+ templates. |
| :---- |

### **What this guide is for**

**Goal:** Help you build the Reference Templates folder — the package of templates and finalized media that the AI Build Pipeline uses to generate your World's synthetic chart files.

By the end of this stage, you'll have:

* **A folder containing the right template for every world-level file in your Section 3 File Plan**  
* **All writer-produced media (EKG tracings, photos, audio) finalized and named correctly**  
* **Everything ready to upload to RL Studio alongside your World Spec at Step 4**

**Why this matters:** Engineering's build pipeline doesn't know what your World needs. The Reference Templates folder is how you tell it. Without the right templates, engineering can't generate realistic files — and your World fails AutoQC at Step 5\.

| 💡 The recipe analogy. Think of your templates as recipes. You pick the right recipe for each dish on the menu (your World Spec). Some recipes come from a standard cookbook (the DataBank). Some you write yourself. Some are standard government forms. A few items — clinical photos, audio recordings, EKG tracings — you prepare yourself because they require your domain expertise. |
| :---- |

⚠️ **Use OPUS for the Claude Project session in this guide.** Sonnet doesn't have enough power for the template curation work. If you get stuck on any step, ping your pod lead in Slack.

## **Types of world-level files you will encounter**

Before diving into the steps, here is a quick reference for the four types of files and who handles what:

| Category | Who creates it | Engineering converts? | Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **DataBank template** | Claude extracts from the DataBank verbatim | Yes | Progress note, discharge summary, consult note, H\&P |
| **Custom-made template** | Writer drafts (Claude can help). Still a template, not a final file. | Yes | Institution-specific pre-op template, hospital P\&L Excel template, specialty clinic note format |
| **Public domain files** | Writer downloads the official blank form from the source agency; or public domain photos from the web | Yes  | FMLA form (Dept. of Labor), USCIS I-693 immigration physical, OSHA injury log; medical/public health photos from the CDC’s website or WHO (screenshotted to remove meta data) |
| **Writer-produced file (not a template)** | Writer creates the actual finalized file using specialty tools | No (already done) | Custom EKG tracing (clinical data simulator), pill bottle photo (NanoBanana Pro), ambient scribe audio (ElevenLabs) |

| Key takeaway. The first three categories are templates/forms that engineering will convert into realistic synthetic files. The fourth category is the small number of files you finalize yourself because they require your clinical domain expertise. All four categories get uploaded to RL Studio together. |
| :---- |

# ▶️ Multimodal Files

## **How to Include Multimodal Data into Your World**

## **🎶 Audio-based Files**

Our project also encourages experts to incorporate high-fidelity realistic inputs into their clinical workflow, which can include audio files. Examples of clinically related audio files that are typically seen in the clinical environment include: audio recordings of conversations (from ambient Ai scribe), cardiopulmonary sounds (wheezing, murmurs, etc.), sounds on abdominal exam, etc.

* [Pulmonary Sound files folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1V7jfyF9vZXPs_jR4bsPjnxoz1C53coPM?usp=drive_link)  
* [Cardiac Sound files folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FgbPoBXBi8_H7g6J_7Co1huaqo2hZhQF?usp=drive_link)

Note that RL Studio is undergoing technical fixes to ensure that it can consistently and reliably interpret audio files. This means that tasks that rely on world-level sound files for self-containment may not be included yet in the next 1-2 weeks (as of 05/23/2026). Workarounds in the meantime are encouraged (i.e. transcripts of conversation vs. raw audio recording).

## **🌐 Public Domain Files**

While **public-domain images** are permitted, please ensure all embedded metadata is scrubbed prior to submission. A simple method is to capture a **screenshot** of the asset (using Snipping Tool or Cmd+Shift+4) and utilize that version. To maintain compliance, **avoid copying and pasting directly from web sources**.

We recommend sourcing images from **reputable medical or educational repositories**. This includes governmental and academic bodies (e.g., NIH, CDC, WHO) or established open-access platforms like **Life in the Fast Lane (LITFL)** and **Radiopaedia**, provided the specific file is licensed for reuse.

Assets must be verified for reuse (e.g., public domain or Creative Commons). To ensure high-fidelity compliance, verify the licensing terms on the source site—specifically searching for labels such as **“public domain”** or **“CC BY-SA.”** If the licensing status is ambiguous, please refrain from using the image.

When in doubt, **err on the side of caution** and select an alternative source.

![][image27]

### ![][image28]![][image29]

### **How to Use the Generators in Your Workflow**

1. **Identify the clinical data needed.** Review your World Spec and task prompts. What documents would realistically exist at each task’s timepoint?

2. **Configure the simulator.** Open the appropriate tool and set parameters to match your patient’s clinical scenario.

3. **Export and annotate.** Export the generated file. Add a text-based interpretation or report that accompanies the visual data.

4. **Embed traps in the data.** Clinical data files are prime trap locations (e.g., a borderline prolonged QTc when the patient is about to start a QT-prolonging medication).

5. **Obtain approval for specialized files.** Confirm with your team lead before including specialized waveform or imaging files.

### **Tool Use: Clinical Calculators & Real-Time Search**

Some tasks should test whether the AI agent can appropriately **use external tools** as part of its clinical reasoning. Examples:

* **Clinical risk calculators:** A task requiring the agent to calculate a HEART score using data scattered across multiple documents.

* **Drug interaction checks:** A medication list with a subtle but clinically significant interaction the agent should flag unprompted.

* **Real-time web search:** A task where the correct answer depends on current clinical guidelines that differ from older guidelines embedded in the chart.

* **Literature retrieval:** A task requiring the agent to cite a specific clinical trial or guideline to justify a treatment recommendation.

| Design principle: Tool use should never be the entire task — it should be one component of a larger clinical workflow. The agent should recognize when a tool is needed, use it correctly, and integrate the result into its clinical reasoning. |
| :---- |

### **O*nly files and images available in the public domain are permitted for use. Please ensure all materials are free of copyright restrictions before using them.***

# **Template/Reference File Additional Resources**

# **Appendix A. How the pipeline works**

This section explains the relationship between your templates and the synthetic files engineering produces.

| The recipe analogy. Think of your templates as recipes. You pick the right recipe for each dish on the menu (your World Spec). Some recipes come from a standard cookbook (the DataBank). Some you write yourself. Some are standard government forms. And a few items, like clinical photos or audio recordings, you prepare yourself because they require your domain expertise. You hand your collection of recipes to a professional kitchen (engineering, via RL Studio). The kitchen produces realistic-looking dishes (synthetic clinical files) with real patient names, dates, and clinical language. The recipe stays generic; the dish is specific. |
| :---- |

# **Appendix B. How file naming works**

**Your World Spec has two relevant columns for every file row:**

* **Filename.type** \= the FINAL synthetic filename engineering produces. Includes a datestamp. Example: ProgressNote.05.11.2023.docx

* **Reference File Origin** \= where the template comes from. No datestamp. Example: DB\_Progress\_Note\_Inpatient.docx

| What you upload | ... | What engineering produces |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| ProgressNoteTemplate.docx | becomes | ProgressNote.05.11.2023.docx |
| FMLA\_Form\_DeptofLabor\_Blank..docx | becomes | FMLA\_Form\_Signed\_08.11.2023..docx |
| HogwartsHospital\_Pre-OP\_Template.docx | becomes | PreOp.Note.09.11.2025.docx |
| HandwrittenMedList.05.15.2019.png | unchanged | HandwrittenMedList.05.15.2019.png |

| Rule of thumb. If engineering will transform the file, your template name is generic (no date). If you finalized the file yourself and it will not change, name it with the final synthetic name (including date) from the Filename.type column. |
| :---- |

# **Appendix C. Detailed Claude Project walkthrough**

### **Setting up a Claude Project**

A Claude Project is a workspace on claude.ai where you can save files and have ongoing conversations. If your pod lead set one up for you, open it and skip ahead.

1. Go to claude.ai and sign in with your Mercor expert email.

2. Click "Projects" in the left sidebar.

3. Click "Create Project" or the "+" icon.

4. Name it: World \[Your World ID\] Templates.

5. Click into the project to open it.

### **How installments work**

After you paste the prompt, Claude will read your spec and DataBank, then work through rows in batches of 3 to 5, pausing to check in with you between batches. Your job is to answer check-in questions promptly and accurately.

### **Example check-in**

| Claude says: I have processed EW1 through EW3. Two items need your input. (1) EW4 is labeled "pre-op anesthesia note" with Reference File Origin set to "DataBank." I see two candidates: DB\_PreOp\_Anesthesia\_Clearance.docx and DB\_PreOp\_Cardiac\_Risk\_Assessment.docx. Which one? (2) WS2 is marked Custom made (orthopedic post-op rehab protocol). Draft from scratch, or do you have a reference to paste? You respond: (1) Use DB\_PreOp\_Anesthesia\_Clearance.docx. (2) Draft from scratch using a generic post-op rehab structure. |
| :---- |

### **Self-QC checklist**

* Every row in the World File plan tables has a matching file in your folder.

* Every file traces back to a row. No orphans.

* Template filenames match the Reference File Origin column (generic, no datestamp).

* Writer-produced filenames match the Filename.type column (final name, with datestamp).

* Media artifacts are finalized, not placeholder stubs.

* No stray, empty, or duplicate files.

# 4️⃣ World Summary

## **Section 4: World Summary**

**→ World Spec Template, Section 4: World Summary**

This is the **final section** of your World Spec — a short wrap-up that captures what your World tests and why it's designed the way it is. Once Sections 1–3 are in place, the Summary is a 3–5 sentence anchor that orients any reader (or reviewer) to your World at a glance.

Section 4 lives at the very end of the World Spec, after the File Plan (Section 3). Claude can draft it from the rest of your Spec — your job is to confirm it captures the design rationale and reads cleanly.

| ⚠   3–5 sentences. Resist the urge to over-write. The World Summary is not a re-statement of your Big Picture Summary (1.1). 1.1 describes the *patient and clinical context*; Section 4 describes the *world design* — what your tasks collectively test, what makes the trap architecture work, and why this world is hard for an AI agent to navigate. |
| :---- |

##  **Claude can draft Section 4 from your Sections 1–3. Your job: confirm it captures the design rationale.**

| ⚠ Review the key concepts and examples present here. However, all of your world spec work should take place in [Sanctum Coach]() which will ensure you understand key concepts and work with you to create world spec \+ templates. |
| :---- |

| What | Claude does | You do |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Drafting the summary | Drafts 3–5 sentences synthesizing Sections 1–3 | Confirm it captures what your World tests \+ why the trap architecture works |
| What the world tests | Pulls from your Section 2 tasks (workflow mix, task types) | Verify it accurately reflects the breadth of clinical reasoning your tasks demand |
| Why traps work | Identifies trap architecture patterns from Section 2 Failure Design \+ Section 3 file plan | Verify the trap rationale is captured — not just the trap list |
| Why it's hard for AI | Articulates from your Complexity Overview (1.5) \+ Failure Design | Confirm it speaks to AI-specific difficulty, not just generic clinical complexity |

## **What the World Summary should cover**

**A 3–5 sentence paragraph that answers three questions:**

1. What clinical or regulatory reasoning does this world test? (medication reconciliation under cascading complications / VA disability nexus reasoning / multi-specialty discharge coordination / etc.)

2. What makes the trap architecture effective? (cross-document reasoning required / specialist friction with attending resolution / temporal contamination / etc.)

3. Why is this world hard for an AI agent to navigate? (information distributed across 25 files / no single source of truth / requires synthesis across timeline)

## **Example (from World 004\)**

| "This world tests an OEM physician's ability to render VA disability nexus opinions across 38 years of fragmented service and clinical records. The trap architecture works through (1) cross-document reconciliation across DD-214s, STR extracts, and PCP visit notes spanning 2008–2023; (2) coding-system friction between ICD-10, VASRD, and ICD-11 classifications; (3) regulatory ambiguity between 38 CFR and PACT Act presumptive criteria. Together, the 8 tasks force the agent to reason across a fragmented, multi-decade chart and apply specialty-specific regulatory logic — work that's hard for AI because reasoning depth, document breadth, and source-of-truth ranking are all in tension." |
| :---- |

# 5️⃣ Synthetic Generation Pipeline

## **World File Generation and Editing Overview**

Here is the full sequence from start to finish for creating the world files.

**Synthetic generation:**  
The world spec you created is fed into a synthetic generation pipeline that will make the world files based on your templates.

**File editing:**  
You take the files that were created and review them along with the AutoQC results. You edit the files to address AutoQC flags and to clean up anything that stands out as off to you. **Remember, these files will be the foundation of all of your tasks, so it’s important to ensure they are really strong\!** They must support the tasks you plan to create.

*Quick checklist for reviewing files:*

* Verify clinical content (dates, names, doses, consistency across documents).  
* Confirm intended trap content survived generation.  
* Identify and correct any new inconsistencies or errors.

**Upload revisions:**  
Upload all the files (edited and unedited) to Studio. Make sure to remove any task files during this process. **Any files uploaded will be in your finished world, so if you leave task-level files, you will run into errors during tasking.**

**Final QC and world creation:**  
Run a final file AutoQC over your newly revised world files. If you see any legitimate flags, you will have to do another round of editing to address them. Check with your reviewer if you are unsure if AutoQC flags are valid or not. **It is important to make sure you are 100% confident in your world files before continuing\!**

Once your files are good to go, you can finalize and create your world\! Please name your world according to the following format: “Healthcare\_\[Patient Last Name\]\_\[\#\#\#\].” For the \#\#\#, pick the next number available based on the number of worlds in Studio.
