## **![][image75]**

**Uploading to RL Studio**

All major deliverables (brainstorm, world spec, template files, world-level files, task prompts, task-level files, golden responses, grader guidelines) are uploaded through RL Studio. The engineering team will also automatically extract your world spec and template files directly from RL Studio in order to produce the world-level (i.e. synthetic) files. 

After uploading each major deliverable, there will also be an AutoQC checker that will flag items as you go through the production pipeline. In order for you to move on to the next step in RL Studio, you must address each AutoQC audit item. 

**Close the Loop on Slack**

As a general best practice, update your pod leads/reviewer accordingly in Slack after each meaningful upload or milestone (brainstorm submission, world spec submission, task packaging, QA work, etc.) to confirm and flag anything that needs reviewer attention. 

# 💻 Claude Best Practices

# **Claude Best Practices**

Treat Claude the way you would treat a resident who has broad medical knowledge but has never worked in your specific practice setting. You would not hand them a blank page and ask them to design a patient case. You would share your thinking, ask them to challenge it, and use their questions to sharpen your own reasoning.

The template was designed to be Claude-friendly. Using Claude to draft your world spec is not just permitted — it is how most experienced writers on this project work efficiently.

## **Where to Use It vs. Where Not To**

| Use Claude for: |
| :---- |

| Use Case | How | Why It Works |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Testing your traps** | Feed Claude your documents and prompt to see if it falls for them. | If Claude doesn’t fall for the trap, it may be too obvious. If it does, you know the trap is functioning. |
| **Consistency auditing** | Paste all essential documents and ask Claude to identify every contradiction. Compare against your intentional contradiction log. | Catches unintentional inconsistencies across your file set that you might miss on manual review. |
| **Drafting from precedents** | Give Claude a real clinical document to adapt rather than asking it to draft from scratch. | Claude-generated clinical documents from blank pages consistently contain generic content that lack the specificity of real drafting. |
| **Drafting the world spec** | Fill in the Writer Input Template yourself, then use Claude to turn your inputs into structured spec format. (See the World Spec section for the full 5-step process.) | Claude handles the mechanical assembly; you provide the clinical judgment. |
| **Pressure-testing your ideas** | Explicitly ask: "Is this task too easy?" "Does this file earn its place?" "What is the plausible wrong answer, and why would a careful clinician reach it?" | Claude won’t push back unless you ask it to. Use it as a sparring partner, not a yes-man. |

| Do NOT use Claude for: |
| :---- |

**These are hard limits — not judgment calls.**

* Task prompts  
* Golden responses  
* Grader guidelines  
* QA responses, failure analyses, or preference labels

Check clinical values for consistency, cross-references between documents for accuracy, and that clinical decisions reflect actual practice in your specialty and clinical setting. You remain responsible for everything in your world regardless of how it was produced.

Use this when you want the reasoning behind each step. # ❓ FAQs

# **FAQs**

**Q:** **I am new. Should I start by writing a world spec from scratch?**

No. Follow the onboarding path: Step 1 — read 2–3 completed example world specs to understand different approaches and the quality bar. Step 2 — start working on your brainstorm. Step 3 — work on your world spec.

**Q: Can I use Claude to write my world spec?**

Yes — and it is encouraged. You must use Claude. You can use Claude to brainstorm patient scenarios, expand bullet-point outlines into full world specs and check for consistency across files. You cannot use Claude to write task prompts, golden responses, grader guidelines, QA responses, or preference labels. The world spec template was specifically designed to be Claude-friendly.

**Q:** **I cannot access files that were shared with me. What should I do?**

Contact the EPMs to request access.

**Q: Who is the world spec written for — engineering's pipeline or other clinicians?**

Both. Engineering's synthetic generation pipeline auto-extracts your spec and your Reference Templates folder to generate the actual world files. Other clinicians may later read your spec to understand the scenario well enough to add tasks to your world. Write it to be precise enough for an automated pipeline to build from and clear enough for a clinician who has never seen your case to design tasks against it.

**Q: Do tasks need to be sequential? Can I create multi-step tasks?**

No, tasks do not need to be sequential. Each task is standalone — the agent tackles it independently with access to the world files and does not carry over context from a previous task. Multi-step tasks are not in scope for now.

**Q; What if a later task needs information that is not in the world files? Can I update the world files?**

No. World files are static after creation. If a new task requires additional clinical information — a new wound assessment, an urgent care intake form, a family member's handwritten medication list — add it as a task-level input file attached to that specific task. Do not modify or expand the shared world file set, as this would break earlier tasks that were designed against the original files.

**Q: How realistic should the prompts be?**

Very. Imagine you are a human expert who received this prompt plus these files. Would you have enough context to do the work, or would you have unanswered questions? If the former, it's fair. If you would need to make assumptions to proceed, the prompt needs work.

**Q: How do we think about difficulty?**

One useful proxy is time: how long would a human expert take to complete this task? In most cases, the answer should be several hours.

Another approach is to review a sample of trajectories and assess whether they contain meaningful deficiencies—errors that a domain expert would consider significant in a real professional context.

Ultimately, difficulty is secondary to realism. The goal is to create tasks that reflect the complexity and nuance of real-world work.

**Q: Why are we moving away from rubric-based grading?**

Overly prescriptive grading requires prompts to be unrealistically specific to be gradeable. A real attending would simply say "write the discharge summary for this patient" and expect competent judgment on what that requires. Rigid rubrics force us to add instructions no supervising physician would actually give, producing artificial prompts. The agentic approach lets you write realistic tasks without worrying about whether a rubric can capture the quality of the output.

**Q: What does "high confidence" mean for preference labels?**

The goal is that a large group of human experts, given the task-specific guidelines, would agree on which output is better. It does not mean 100% inter-rater agreement — that is not feasible. It means your label should be defensible to a senior physician reading your justification. If you cannot articulate a specific clinical or administrative difference that drove your decision, reconsider the label.

# **Claude FAQ**

This section covers the most common issues writers encounter during the template and reference file workflow. If your question is not answered here, ask your pod lead or reviewer in Slack.

## **Claude Project and setup**

### **I cannot find "Projects" in Claude.**

Make sure you are signed in at claude.ai (not a different Claude interface). Projects is in the left sidebar. If you do not see it, your account may not have access. Ask your pod lead to confirm your account is set up correctly.

### **I do not know which email to use for Claude.**

Use your Mercor expert email. This is the same email you use for RL Studio and Google Drive. If you are unsure which email that is, check with your pod lead.

### **Claude says it cannot read one of my files.**

Confirm the file is a .docx (not .doc, .docx, or .pages). If the file is very large, try re-saving it as a fresh .docx. If the problem persists, ask your pod lead.

## **Working with Claude**

### **Claude is producing everything at once instead of working in installments.**

The system prompt instructs Claude to work in installments. If Claude ignores this, paste the following reminder: "Please work in installments of 3 to 5 rows. Pause and check in with me after each batch before continuing."

### **Claude is going faster than I can keep up with.**

Tell Claude to pause. Example: "Pause. Let me review EW1 to EW3 before you continue. I will tell you when to proceed."

### **Claude asks a question I do not understand.**

Ask Claude to rephrase: "I do not understand your question. Can you rephrase it in simpler terms?" If it is still unclear, copy the question and paste it to your pod lead in Slack for help.

### **Claude produced a template that does not match what I had in mind.**

Tell Claude exactly which row and what to fix. Example: "For EW3, the template you produced is an inpatient progress note but my spec describes an outpatient clinic visit. Please redo EW3 using DB\_Progress\_Note\_Outpatient.docx instead." You do not have to start over; Claude can redo individual rows.

### **Claude seems to be making up content that is not in the DataBank.**

The system prompt tells Claude never to fabricate. If you suspect Claude is inventing a template rather than extracting from the DataBank, ask: "Is this template from the DataBank, or did you draft it from scratch? If you drafted it, which row in my spec required a custom-made template?" If the issue persists, flag it to your pod lead.

### **My Claude session timed out or got cut off in the middle of a batch.**

Start a new chat in the same Claude Project. Re-attach all three files and paste the prompt starter again. Then tell Claude where you left off: "We were working on my world-level files. You already completed EW1 through EW5. Please continue from WS1."

### **Claude is using em dashes, en dashes, or AI-sounding phrasing.**

Remind it: "Please do not use em dashes, en dashes, or AI-sounding phrasing in any template you produce. Use plain hyphens or restructure the sentence."

### **Claude produced a file I cannot open.**

Make sure you have Microsoft Word or Google Docs available. Claude produces .docx files. If the file appears corrupted, ask Claude to regenerate it: "The file for EW3 appears corrupted. Please regenerate it."

## **DataBank and templates**

### **The DataBank template I named does not exist.**

Open the DataBank and search for the template by keyword (not exact filename). You may have misspelled the filename in your spec. If no match exists, decide whether to use a different DataBank template, mark the row as custom-made, or ask your pod lead for guidance.

### **Two DataBank templates seem similar. Which one do I use?**

Open both templates and read through them. Pick the one that more closely matches the clinical document described in your spec row. If you are still unsure, ask your pod lead or reviewer.

### **The DataBank does not have a template for my specialty.**

Mark the row as custom-made in the Reference File Origin column. Claude can help you draft the template from scratch, or you can use the custom template generator as a starting point. If your specialty is frequently underrepresented, flag it to your pod lead so the DataBank can be updated for future writers.

### **A DataBank template looks outdated or has errors.**

Do not fix it yourself. Flag the specific template and the issue to your pod lead in Slack. Use the template as-is for now unless your pod lead tells you otherwise.

## **File naming**

### **The template filename does not match the Filename.type in my spec.**

That is correct and expected. The Filename.type column is the final synthetic filename engineering will produce (with a datestamp). The template filename is generic (no datestamp). Do not rename your templates. See Appendix B for the full explanation.

### **I do not know what to name my custom-made template.**

Use a descriptive name that makes it obvious what the document is. Follow the pattern: what it is \+ where it is from. Examples: HogwartsHospital\_Pre-OP\_Template.docx, CardiacRehab\_ProgressNote\_Template.docx. No datestamps on templates.

### **I do not know what to name my writer-produced file.**

Writer-produced files that will NOT go through engineering should use the final synthetic filename (WITH datestamp) from the Filename.type column in your spec. Example: HandwrittenMedList.05.15.2019.png.

### **I accidentally renamed a template to match the Filename.type column.**

Rename it back to the generic template name (no datestamp). If you are unsure what the original name was, check the Reference File Origin column in your spec or ask Claude to remind you.

## **Writer-produced files**

### **I am not sure if a file should be writer-produced or a template.**

Ask yourself: can an engineer who is not a physician produce a realistic version of this file from a template? If yes, it is a template for engineering. If it requires your clinical domain expertise, specialty knowledge, or a tool like Nano Banana Pro or ElevenLabs to create, it is writer-produced. If still unsure, ask your pod lead.

### **I do not know how to use Nano Banana Pro / ElevenLabs / the clinical data generators.**

Refer to the clinical data generators guide linked in Step 3\. If you need additional help with a specific tool, ask your pod lead or reviewer. They can walk you through it or point you to a tutorial.

### **I produced a file but I am not sure if it is good enough to submit.**

Open the file and ask: does this look like a realistic version of what it is supposed to represent? If it is a pill bottle photo, does it look like an actual pill bottle? If it is an EKG tracing, would a clinician recognize it as plausible? If you are unsure, share it with your pod lead or reviewer for a quick gut check before uploading.

### **Claude reminded me about writer-produced files I have not created yet.**

This is the system prompt working as intended. Claude tracks which rows are writer-produced and reminds you before you finish. Produce those files using the appropriate tools, add them to your folder, and include them when you upload to RL Studio.

## **World Spec and Reference File Origin**

### **I am confused about the Reference File Origin column.**

The Reference File Origin column tells Claude (and engineering) where each template comes from. For each row, you write one of: the DataBank template filename, Custom made (brief description), Public Domain (form name: source agency), or Writer-produced (brief description, tool). See Step 3 for examples of each.

### **I am not sure which origin to pick for a particular row.**

Start with the DataBank. Open it and search for a template that fits. If nothing fits, decide whether the document is a standard government form (public domain) or something you need to outline yourself (custom-made). If the file requires clinical expertise or specialty tools (photos, audio, tracings), mark it as writer-produced. When in doubt, ask your pod lead.

### **I am not sure if a row is world-level or task-level.**

World-level files are shared across all tasks in the world. Task-level files are specific to a single task. If the file would appear in every clinical encounter for this patient, it is likely world-level. If it is specific to one encounter, it is likely task-level. This guide covers world-level files only. If unsure, ask your pod lead.

### **I accidentally changed the World Spec template structure.**

Revert to the original template and re-enter your content. Engineering's pipeline reads the spec programmatically, so structural changes (renamed columns, rearranged sections, deleted headings) will break file generation. Compare your version to a clean copy of the template or ask your pod lead.

## **Self-QC**

### **I found a mismatch between my spec and my folder.**

Fix it before uploading. If a row in your spec has no matching file, produce or obtain the file. If a file in your folder has no matching row, either add the row to your spec or remove the file. Mismatches are the most common reason a package is returned for rework.

### **My file count does not match my row count.**

Walk through your spec row by row and check off each file as you find it in your folder. Identify which rows are missing files and which files are orphans. Fix each one. If a single row maps to two paired templates (e.g., discharge instructions plus medication list), both files count.

### **I am not sure if my package is complete.**

Run the self-QC checklist in Appendix C. If everything checks out, your package is complete. If you are still uncertain, share your folder and spec with your pod lead for a quick review before uploading.

## **RL Studio upload**

### **I cannot access RL Studio.**

Confirm you are using your Mercor expert email. If you still cannot log in, ask your pod lead to verify your access.

### **I do not know how to upload individual files.**

Refer to the RL Studio upload guide linked in Step 6\. If you are still stuck, ask your pod lead to walk you through it. Each file is a separate upload; do not package into a zip.

### **I uploaded the wrong files and need to fix my submission.**

Contact your pod lead immediately. They can advise whether you need to re-upload or whether the submission can be corrected in place.

### **I finished uploading. What do I do next?**

Post in your pod channel confirming the package is complete and tag your pod lead or reviewer. Engineering picks up the package from RL Studio and produces the synthetic files. You do not need to do anything further unless engineering or your reviewer comes back with questions.

## **General**

### **I am stuck and do not know who to ask.**

Your pod lead is your first point of contact for any question about the workflow. If your pod lead is unavailable, tag your reviewer. If neither responds within a reasonable time, escalate in the team-wide Slack channel.

### **I am confused about the overall workflow.**

Re-read Steps 1 through 6 at the top of this guide. The workflow is: brainstorm approved, draft spec, fill in file plan tables, use Claude to assemble templates, self-QC, upload to RL Studio. If a specific step is unclear, ask your pod lead to walk you through it.

### **This is my first world. Is there someone who can review my work before I submit?**

Yes. Your pod lead and reviewer are there to help, especially on your first world. Share your folder and spec with them before uploading to RL Studio. They can catch issues early and save you rework.
